classification_signals: The paper explicitly states 'In this chapter I consider several versions of what we can call the extended body hypothesis.' (Abstract, p. 1)

It synthesizes findings from numerous cited empirical studies (e.g., Iriki et al. 1996, Cardinali et al. 2009a/b, Yamamoto and Kitazawa 2001a/b, Botvinick and Cohen 1998, Hohwy and Paton 2010, Miyazaki et al. 2010, Guterstam et al. 2013, von Békésy 1959/1967) to build its arguments.
The structure involves presenting a hypothesis, reviewing evidence for and against it, and drawing conclusions, characteristic of a narrative review or theoretical paper.
No new empirical data or methods section for an original experiment is presented by the authors.

minimum_safe_summary: This narrative review explores the 'extended body hypothesis,' examining how bodily awareness can extend beyond biological and even apparent bodily boundaries. It synthesizes evidence showing that tools can be incorporated into sensorimotor and perceptual body representations, allowing for direct tactile sensations in them. However, the paper argues that tools are not 'affectively embodied,' meaning intransitive sensations like pain, itches, and tickles cannot be felt in them, which is crucial for maintaining a stable, default representation of the biological body. The review also discusses how sensations can be experienced in peripersonal space, even outside apparent bodily boundaries, but emphasizes that these are still localized relative to a bodily frame of reference. A key limitation highlighted is the need for further development in understanding the relationship between pain, affective embodiment, and the sense of bodily ownership.

paper_metadata.title: The Extended Body Hypothesis
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract:
Abstract
               According to the extended mind hypothesis, “There is nothing sacred about skull and skin” for our cognitive abilities (Clark and Chalmers 1998). Is this also true for bodily awareness? In this chapter I consider several versions of what we can call the extended body hypothesis. According to a weak version, bodily awareness is not limited by the biological boundaries of our body. In light of tool embodiment, I highlight the malleability of embodiment but also show that there are important limitations to the sensations that we can feel in tools. I then consider a stronger version of the extended body hypothesis, according to which bodily awareness is not even constrained by the apparent boundaries of the body. I will describe how we can experience sensations in peripersonal space, but argue that even then there seems to be something sacred about our apparent skull and skin.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Tools become incorporated into the body schema, dynamically extending peripersonal space and influencing sensory processing, leading to referred sensations.

mechanism_chain.description: The brain integrates sensory and motor information from tool use, leading to a dynamic remapping of peripersonal space and changes in sensory processing.
